paragraphs: An image estimator can be accurate in its pixel values while producing outputs whose overall statistics differ from those of natural images. This paper studies that tension mathematically: how little reconstruction error is possible when the output distribution must meet a specified perceptual requirement? It measures reconstruction error using mean squared error and distributional mismatch using Wasserstein-2 distance.

For this particular pairing of measures, the authors derive a closed-form expression for the optimal distortion–perception tradeoff. They prove that the function is quadratic regardless of the underlying data distribution. Their explanation is geometric: estimators along the optimal tradeoff trace a geodesic, a shortest-path structure in Wasserstein space.

The paper also explains how to construct optimal estimators. In the Gaussian case, it supplies explicit formulas. For general distributions, it connects intermediate solutions to two endpoints: the unconstrained mean squared-error minimizer and the best estimator whose outputs perfectly match the target distribution. The latter can be built through a stochastic transformation of the former, linking distributional realism to an existing error-minimizing estimator.
neurips-2021-a-theory-of-the-distortion-.tldr: The paper derives an exact quadratic tradeoff between mean squared reconstruction error and Wasserstein-2 perceptual quality, with constructions for optimal estimators.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive black-box function often means deciding both where to evaluate it and how accurately to do so. Cheaper, lower-fidelity evaluations can provide useful information, but their relationship to accurate evaluations may be complicated. BMBO-DARN addresses this setting while choosing batches of evaluations, aiming to obtain more optimization benefit for the evaluation cost.

The method builds a surrogate from Bayesian neural networks arranged in a fully autoregressive structure. This lets the model represent complex dependencies across fidelity levels. Its batch acquisition function follows the Max-value Entropy Search principle and penalizes highly correlated queries, encouraging a batch to contain complementary information instead of repeatedly asking similar questions.

To make query selection practical, the authors use posterior samples and moment matching to compute the acquisition function efficiently. They alternate optimization over fidelity–input pairs without a combinatorial search over fidelity assignments, guaranteeing improvement at each optimization step. Experiments on four real-world hyperparameter optimization applications demonstrate advantages for the approach, supporting the combination of expressive fidelity modeling and diversity-aware batch selection.
neurips-2021-batch-multi-fidelity-bayesi.tldr: BMBO-DARN combines neural models of relationships across evaluation fidelities with diverse batch selection for cost-conscious Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: The paper considers selecting at most k elements from n candidates to maximize a monotone submodular objective. Such objectives reward adding elements but exhibit diminishing returns as the selected set grows. The computational challenge is to obtain a strong solution while limiting both the number of objective queries and the sequential rounds that prevent parallel execution.

The proposed algorithm combines two procedures. LINEARSEQ preprocesses the problem to reduce query requirements and can also help other algorithms. A variant has adaptive complexity logarithmic in n/k. THRESHOLDSEQ provides a parallelizable way to add elements whose gains exceed a fixed threshold. Together, these components support efficient selection without requiring every decision to be made sequentially.

The main result combines an approximation ratio close to 1−1/e, logarithmic adaptivity, and an expected linear number of queries, with high-probability guarantees as stated in the paper. In a comprehensive evaluation using six submodular objectives, the method outperforms FAST on runtime, adaptive rounds, query count, and achieved objective value. These results connect theoretical efficiency with practical performance on the evaluated problems.
neurips-2021-best-of-both-worlds-practic.tldr: A parallel submodular maximization algorithm combines strong approximation guarantees with few queries and adaptive rounds, and outperforms FAST in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian neural networks can underfit, and their predictions can depend strongly on the prior distribution assigned to their weights. A common response is to fix the prior's parameters at conventional values or tune them separately. This paper instead makes those parameters part of the probabilistic model, allowing uncertainty about them to enter the inference procedure.

The authors extend the model and collapse the variational bound with respect to the posterior distributions of the prior parameters. This produces tighter evidence lower bounds, or ELBOs, which serve as training objectives for variational inference. The central change is therefore in how the learning objective handles the prior, rather than simply choosing another fixed prior setting.

Experiments across multiple datasets show significant improvements for Gaussian mean-field variational inference, including in deep networks. These results demonstrate that this relatively simple approximation can perform well with the proposed objectives. The authors also find that the tighter bounds can be useful for learning hyperparameters of hierarchical priors, connecting improved predictive training with a more principled way to adjust the prior structure.
neurips-2021-collapsed-variational-bound.tldr: Treating prior parameters probabilistically yields tighter variational objectives that improve Bayesian neural-network performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation when an oblivious adversary can corrupt responses in all but an α fraction of observations. The goal is consistency: estimation error should approach zero as more observations become available. The authors develop efficiently computable estimators for sparse regression and principal component analysis, addressing settings in which reliable observations may be a small minority.

Their construction combines the Huber loss with nonsmooth regularizers, including the ℓ1 norm and nuclear norm. For sparse regression, they obtain optimal sample-size scaling of roughly k log(d)/α² and an optimal error rate proportional to the square root of k log(d)/(nα²). Here k measures sparsity, d is dimension, and n is the observation count. The analysis allows the inlier fraction to be inverse-polynomial in sample size.

For PCA, the authors establish optimal error guarantees under broad assumptions controlling matrix spikiness. They also prove statistical lower bounds showing that the inlier fraction their PCA estimator tolerates is optimal up to a constant factor. Together, the results explain when strong corruption can coexist with accurate estimation under the stated adversarial and structural assumptions.
neurips-2021-consistent-estimation-for-p.tldr: Regularized Huber-loss estimators achieve consistent sparse regression and PCA under severe oblivious corruption, with optimal guarantees in the stated settings.

paragraphs: When a critical class has few training examples, overall classification accuracy can hide costly mistakes. Detecting a high proportion of critical cases can also produce many false alarms among noncritical cases. This paper argues that training should directly prioritize reducing false positives while maintaining a high true positive rate, especially when missing positive cases carries greater cost.

The authors formulate binary neural-network training as a constrained optimization problem. Their proposed constraint can be combined with existing loss functions and targets area under the ROC curve while emphasizing the high-true-positive-rate region. They solve the resulting problem using an Augmented Lagrangian method, bringing the desired operating behavior into training. They also propose two extensions of the constraint for multiclass classification.

Experiments cover an in-house medical imaging dataset, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. In the majority of evaluated cases, the method improves on the baselines by increasing accuracy for critical classes while reducing errors on noncritical samples. The finding supports explicitly training for this balance rather than relying on overall accuracy to reflect performance on rare, consequential cases.
neurips-2021-constrained-optimization-to.tldr: A constrained training objective prioritizes fewer false alarms at high detection rates for critical classes, improving most evaluated cases.

paragraphs: The task here is to identify the m options with the highest average rewards while keeping the probability of an incorrect answer below a chosen level δ. Linear bandit models offer a convenient structure for sharing information across options, but real observations can depart from linear predictions. The paper studies how to make reliable selections despite this misspecification.

The authors first derive a tractable lower bound on the number of samples required by any algorithm meeting the error requirement for general top-m identification. They also show that knowing the scale of deviations from linearity is necessary to exploit the problem's structure. This identifies a concrete information requirement for benefiting from an approximate linear model.

They then propose a practical algorithm that adapts to the amount of misspecification. Its sample-complexity upper bound captures that adaptation and matches the lower bound as δ approaches zero. This is an asymptotic optimality statement in the increasingly stringent confidence regime. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data show competitive performance against existing baselines, connecting the analysis to practical selection problems.
neurips-2021-dealing-with-misspecificati.tldr: An adaptive top-m identification algorithm handles departures from linearity and matches a sample-complexity lower bound as the allowed error probability approaches zero.

paragraphs: Derivatives of a data distribution describe its local structure, with higher-order derivatives providing information beyond the first-order score used in denoising methods. One way to obtain them is to repeatedly differentiate a learned density model. The paper identifies two difficulties with that route: it can magnify estimation errors and become computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings.

The authors instead learn higher-order derivatives directly from samples. They first connect ordinary denoising score matching to Tweedie's formula, then apply that relationship to higher-order moments. This extends the denoising learning principle to quantities that would otherwise be obtained through automatic differentiation. The approach makes those quantities explicit learning targets rather than indirect consequences of another fitted model.

Empirically, the proposed models estimate second-order derivatives more accurately and efficiently than the automatic-differentiation approach. The authors also demonstrate two uses for the learned information: quantifying uncertainty in denoising and improving the mixing speed of Langevin sampling through Ozaki discretization. Sampling experiments include synthetic data and natural images, showing how richer local distributional information can support downstream computations.
neurips-2021-estimating-high-order-gradi.tldr: A generalization of denoising score matching learns higher-order distribution derivatives directly, improving second-order estimation and supporting uncertainty estimation and sampling.

paragraphs: Inductive matrix completion uses side information to help infer missing matrix entries. This paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of how such methods generalize, aiming to bring their guarantees into line with those available for ordinary matrix completion. Its bounds track the dimension d of the side information and the matrix rank r.

For nuclear-norm methods in a distribution-free setting, the authors improve the previously best scaling from O(rd²) to approximately d to the three-halves power times the square root of r, ignoring logarithmic factors. They also introduce a smoothed adjusted trace-norm strategy with guarantees scaling approximately as dr under arbitrary sampling. Previously, a similar inductive rate required uniform sampling and concerned exact recovery.

Both results agree with established bounds when specialized to ordinary matrix completion, where those bounds are tight up to logarithmic terms. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real problems further show that the proposed strategy outperforms standard inductive matrix completion. The contribution thus combines sharper guarantees with evidence that adjusting the regularization strategy can improve completion using side information.
neurips-2021-fine-grained-generalization.tldr: Sharper generalization bounds and an adjusted trace-norm method improve the theory and reported performance of matrix completion with side information.

paragraphs: Liquid state machines offer low training complexity and biological plausibility, making them attractive for neuromorphic and edge computing. Their internal weights are adjusted without backpropagating gradients, but their performance has lagged behind multilayer neural networks. This paper draws inspiration from astrocytes, brain cells that modulate neural plasticity and dynamics, to improve that balance.

The proposed neuron–astrocyte liquid state machine uses an astrocyte model to aggregate neuronal activity and provide global feedback to spike-timing-dependent plasticity. That feedback organizes the network around a critical branching factor associated with the transition between ordered and chaotic activity. The intended benefit is self-organized near-critical dynamics without data-specific manual tuning.

The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among comparable liquid state machine methods: top accuracies of 97.61% on MNIST, 97.51% on N-MNIST, and 85.84% on Fashion-MNIST. These results are comparable to current fully connected multilayer spiking networks trained with backpropagation. The findings suggest that this biologically inspired control mechanism could help advance capable neuromorphic learning, while broader benefits for robust, energy-efficient edge computing remain a stated potential.
neurips-2021-increasing-liquid-state-mac.tldr: Astrocyte-inspired feedback self-organizes a liquid state machine near critical dynamics, improving classification performance without dataset-specific hand-tuning.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must consider the actions taken during learning, as well as the final policy. This paper explores avoiding every training-time safety violation when starting with only a safe policy that earns trivial reward. The setting provides neither prior knowledge of the system dynamics nor additional offline data, making safe improvement particularly challenging.

The proposed CRABS algorithm repeatedly learns three connected components: a dynamics model, a policy, and barrier certificates that certify safety. It learns the certificates through adversarial training and adds regularization that encourages larger certified regions, creating room for exploration. The certificates ensure policy safety under the explicit assumption that the learned dynamics are calibrated.

Simulations show that avoiding violations is challenging even in environments with only two to four state dimensions, especially when rewarding behavior approaches the safety boundary. Prior methods require hundreds of violations to obtain decent rewards on these tasks, whereas the proposed algorithms incur none. These results support the feasibility of the approach in the tested settings, with the stated safety guarantee depending on dynamics calibration.
neurips-2021-learning-barrier-certificat.tldr: CRABS jointly learns safety certificates, dynamics, and policies, achieving zero violations in reported simulations with safety guarantees conditional on calibrated dynamics.

paragraphs: Binary neural networks convert weights and activations to one-bit values using a sign function. This makes training difficult because the function's gradient is zero almost everywhere, leaving backpropagation without a useful learning signal. Existing methods substitute approximate gradients, but the paper argues that these approximations can distort the direction of the intended gradient.

The proposed frequency domain approximation represents the sign function through a combination of sine functions and uses that representation to estimate its gradient. It preserves the low-frequency information, which contains most of the function's overall energy, while leaving out high-frequency coefficients to limit computational cost. A noise adaptation module is included during training to compensate for approximation error.

Experiments across several benchmark datasets and network architectures report state-of-the-art accuracy for the resulting binary networks. The contribution is a training method that uses the frequency structure of the binarization function to construct the learning signal. Its reported gains suggest that both the choice of approximation and compensation for its residual error matter for effective binary-network optimization.
neurips-2021-learning-frequency-domain-a.tldr: Frequency domain approximation trains binary neural networks with a sine-based gradient estimate and error compensation, achieving reported state-of-the-art accuracy.

paragraphs: Holographic Reduced Representations associate abstract concepts with real-valued vectors and provide operations that manipulate those vectors like symbolic objects. This paper revisits the approach as a possible differentiable component inside deep learning. The aim is to combine symbolic structure with neural learning through operations that can participate directly in training.

The authors identify numerical instability as an obstacle to using these representations in a differentiable system. They introduce a projection step that moves the vectors into a better-behaved region of their representation space. With this change, they report more than a hundredfold improvement in concept retrieval efficacy, addressing a central practical weakness of the representation.

The paper then uses the symbolic properties of these vectors to design an output layer and loss function for multilabel classification. The resulting system learns effectively in that application and provides a way to examine advantages and disadvantages of the neural-symbolic approach. The contribution is both a stabilization technique and a concrete demonstration of how symbolic vector operations can be incorporated into a learned prediction system.
neurips-2021-learning-with-holographic-r.tldr: A stabilizing projection makes Holographic Reduced Representations more effective for concept retrieval and usable in a neural-symbolic multilabel classifier.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent may perform a visual task successfully while remaining difficult to interpret. This paper examines that problem by comparing the image regions associated with an agent's decisions to those attended to by human experts performing the same task. The aim is to connect visual representations with behavior, rather than assess performance alone.

The study focuses on Atari games and compares agent saliency maps with models of expert human visual attention. It asks how similar the learned representations are and how their similarities or differences can help explain agent performance. This comparison provides a concrete way to investigate which visual information the trained systems emphasize during task execution.

The authors also analyze how reinforcement-learning hyperparameters affect the learned representations and saliency maps. This links choices made during training to the visual behavior of the resulting agent. The stated contribution is an interpretive investigation whose insights could inform future algorithms for narrowing the performance gap with human experts. The abstract presents that algorithmic benefit as a possibility, rather than reporting that the gap has already been closed.
neurips-2021-machine-versus-human-attent.tldr: The study compares Atari agents' saliency maps with expert human attention to investigate visual representations, performance, and the effects of training hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require enormous amounts of interaction before an agent performs well. This paper targets sample efficiency in learning from images, where achieving consistent human-level Atari performance with little experience has been difficult. The authors introduce EfficientZero, a model-based visual reinforcement-learning algorithm built on MuZero.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, EfficientZero achieves mean performance of 194.3% and median performance of 109.0% relative to human performance, using experience corresponding to two hours of real-time play. These aggregate results put both the mean and median above the human reference. The paper describes this as the first superhuman Atari result with such limited data.

EfficientZero also approaches DQN's performance at 200 million frames while using 500 times less data. On some tasks in the DMControl 100k benchmark, it outperforms state SAC. These findings demonstrate substantial interaction efficiency in the evaluated settings, which the authors connect to the prospect of more practical reinforcement learning. They also provide an implementation intended to make research on Monte Carlo tree search-based reinforcement learning more accessible.
neurips-2021-mastering-atari-games-with-.tldr: EfficientZero achieves above-human mean and median Atari 100k performance with limited experience, demonstrating strong sample efficiency for model-based visual reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Visual scenes contain distinct entities whose properties determine how they interact. The paper argues that modeling these interactions benefits from sparse relationships and a separation between knowledge about particular entities and knowledge about interaction rules. It identifies these as weaknesses of the graph neural networks commonly used for the task.

Neural Production Systems adapt the classical idea of rule templates with placeholders that can be bound to specific entities. The architecture scores how well rules match the available entities, selects the best-fitting rules, and applies them to update entity properties. This creates a flexible flow of computation in which the rules used depend on the current entities.

Experiments show that the architecture separates entity-specific information from rule-based information and supports dynamic control. It achieves robust future-state prediction in rich visual environments, outperforming state-of-the-art graph neural network methods in the reported comparisons. It also supports extrapolation from environments with few objects to more complex ones. These findings connect reusable interaction rules with the ability to predict behavior beyond the simpler environments used for learning.
neurips-2021-neural-production-systems-c.tldr: Neural Production Systems learn entity-conditioned interaction rules that improve visual future-state prediction and support extrapolation to more complex environments.

paragraphs: Symmetry is often used to design neural networks, but this paper asks what happens when the learning process itself breaks a symmetry. The authors develop a theoretical framework for the geometry of training dynamics, seeking to explain mechanisms behind the efficiency and stability of modern networks through ideas from mechanics.

They model discrete gradient-descent dynamics using a continuous-time Lagrangian formulation. In this description, the learning rule plays the role of kinetic energy and the loss plays the role of potential energy. Kinetic symmetry breaking occurs when the former breaks a symmetry of the latter. The authors extend Noether's theorem to this situation and derive how the corresponding Noether charge evolves during learning.

Applying this framework to networks with normalization layers reveals a mechanism of implicit adaptive optimization. The resulting learning dynamics have an analogy to RMSProp, linking architectural normalization to the way optimization adapts during training. The paper's contribution is a theoretical account of that connection and a framework for investigating geometric principles that could guide the design of neural-network learning dynamics.
neurips-2021-noethers-learning-dynamics-.tldr: A mechanics-based analysis shows how symmetry breaking in learning dynamics lets normalization layers induce an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a policy from a fixed dataset when performance involves multiple objectives and behavior must satisfy a constraint. A preference function determines how the objectives are combined. The offline setting matters when collecting new interactions is expensive or violating the constraint could be dangerous, so learning must work with the evidence already available.

The authors reformulate the constrained problem in primal-dual terms and solve it through dual gradient ascent. They combine this approach with pessimism to account for uncertainty in the offline data, producing Pessimistic Dual Iteration, or PEDI. Pessimism is central because uncertain estimates from a fixed dataset must be handled when assessing possible policies.

The analysis provides upper bounds on both performance suboptimality and constraint violation for the learned policy using an arbitrary dataset. The authors establish sample efficiency without assuming dataset coverage and also specialize the method to linear function approximation. These are guarantees that bound the two quantities; they do not claim that every dataset yields an exactly optimal policy with zero constraint violations.
neurips-2021-offline-constrained-multi-o.tldr: PEDI combines primal-dual optimization with pessimism to bound offline multi-objective policy suboptimality and constraint violation without a dataset coverage assumption.

paragraphs: Random-search methods optimize functions by evaluating candidate points without requiring derivatives. For nonconvex objectives, understanding where such methods converge involves more than checking whether the gradient is small. This paper studies convergence to second-order stationary points, which also account for curvature and provide a stronger target than first-order stationarity.

The authors prove that standard random-search methods can reach such points even without explicitly using second-order information. However, their complexity grows exponentially with the number of input dimensions. That result separates the possibility of convergence from its computational practicality: a method may eventually reach the desired type of point while requiring an unfavorable number of evaluations.

To address this dependence, the paper introduces a random-search variant that exploits negative curvature using only function evaluations. Its evaluation complexity depends linearly on dimension, a substantial improvement over the exponential dependence of the standard methods analyzed. Empirical tests agree well with the theoretical findings. The contribution shows how curvature-sensitive search can improve dimension scaling even when derivative information is unavailable.
neurips-2021-on-the-second-order-converg.tldr: A derivative-free random-search method exploits negative curvature to achieve second-order convergence with linear rather than exponential dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Zero-shot action recognition aims to recognize action categories absent from training. A common method maps video into a semantic space and selects the nearest class representation. This paper argues that such a setup is poorly suited to videos containing multiple actions, especially when the actions are semantically distinct but occur together.

The authors replace nearest-neighbor classification with a pairwise scoring function. Given a video and candidate action classes, the model assigns a confidence score to each class independently. This changes the prediction problem so that several distinct actions can receive high confidence for the same video, rather than requiring the representation to select one nearby semantic target.

Evaluation covers both single-label and multilabel recognition. The method shows strong performance on UCF-101, HMDB, and RareAct, and outperforms previous zero-shot approaches on the multilabel AVA dataset and the MEVA surprise activity detection dataset. These results support the usefulness of independent video–class scoring for recognizing co-occurring actions while retaining effectiveness on tasks with a single action label.
neurips-2021-reformulating-zero-shot-act.tldr: Independent video–class scoring enables zero-shot recognition of multiple co-occurring actions and improves results on the reported multilabel and surprise-activity datasets.

paragraphs: Many optimization methods have strong convergence or regret guarantees but repeatedly require expensive projections onto a feasible region. Conditional-gradient methods replace projection with linear optimization, often at the cost of weaker rates. This paper addresses that tradeoff for submodular base polytopes by focusing on repeated projections of points that are close to one another.

The authors develop tools that use both discrete and continuous structure to accelerate these computations. The central opportunity is to reuse relevant structure across nearby projection problems instead of treating each as unrelated. They adapt the away-step Frank-Wolfe algorithm to exploit this information and allow early termination, reducing the work involved in obtaining projections.

For cardinality-based submodular polytopes, the paper proves a runtime improvement of at least order n/log(n) for certain Bregman projections. That result applies to the specified special case rather than every projection problem. Preliminary computational experiments report runtime reductions of orders of magnitude. Together, the theory and experiments suggest that reusing structure can make projection-based optimization substantially more practical in these settings.
neurips-2021-reusing-combinatorial-struc.tldr: Reusing structure across nearby projections accelerates optimization over submodular base polytopes, with a proven speedup for certain cardinality-based cases.

paragraphs: Predicting a set requires deciding which predicted element corresponds to which target element before assigning a training signal. Existing approaches perform this matching in the original feature space using a predefined distance function. This paper proposes learning the matching distance by moving the comparison into a latent space produced by encoding networks.

This change also enables teacher forcing during training. With feature-space matching, the correspondence must be computed after the entire output sequence has been generated, which prevents that training approach. Latent-space matching changes this dependency, making it possible to use teacher forcing while learning a representation suited to matching predicted and target elements.

A naive implementation can still fail to converge because the permutation used to match elements is unstable. The authors provide sufficient conditions for permutation stability and use them to derive an algorithm that improves overall convergence. These conditions establish a route to stability rather than a necessary characterization of every stable method. Experiments on several set-prediction tasks, including image captioning and object detection, demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
neurips-2021-set-prediction-in-the-laten.tldr: Learning set matching in latent space enables teacher forcing, while sufficient permutation-stability conditions guide an algorithm that improves convergence.

paragraphs: Distributed training must exchange information between machines, making communication a major part of optimization cost. Existing techniques include compression, variance reduction, and acceleration. This paper argues that further improvements are possible by exploiting the detailed smoothness structure of each local loss, rather than summarizing that structure with a single smoothness constant.

The authors use smoothness matrices, which retain richer information about how local losses vary. They propose a communication sparsification strategy designed to take advantage of these matrices. The approach connects the information sent during distributed optimization to the structure of the losses being optimized, providing a more informative basis for compression.

To demonstrate the method, the paper adapts it to DCGD, DIANA, and ADIANA. The resulting algorithms achieve significant communication-complexity savings, and the authors report that the new methods consistently outperform their baselines, often by large margins. The stated contribution spans theory and practice: richer descriptions of local smoothness support better communication strategies across three distributed optimization algorithms, rather than only a single specialized procedure.
neurips-2021-smoothness-matrices-beat-sm.tldr: Matrix-valued smoothness information guides communication sparsification that reduces communication complexity for three distributed optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: Models that infer physical dynamics from images are often evaluated by how well they reconstruct the images. This paper shows empirically that reconstruction quality does not always indicate whether the underlying dynamics were learned correctly. It focuses on models informed by Hamiltonian mechanics, where known physical structure can support a more direct evaluation.

The authors develop several measures, including SyMetric, a binary indicator intended to assess whether the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics have been faithfully captured. These measures use properties of Hamiltonian systems and distinguish dynamics-learning quality more effectively than reconstruction error. The evaluation target therefore includes the structure of the learned motion, beyond the appearance of individual reconstructions.

Using SyMetric, the authors identify architectural changes that significantly improve the Hamiltonian Generative Network. The reported results include physically meaningful latent representations on some datasets and substantially longer stable rollouts across a collection of 13 datasets. On a subset, forward and backward rollouts remain effectively unlimited without quality degradation. These qualified findings illustrate how a dynamics-focused metric can guide improvements in both interpretability and long-term prediction.
neurips-2021-symetric-measuring-the-qual.tldr: SyMetric evaluates learned Hamiltonian structure more directly than image reconstruction and helps identify architectures with more interpretable and stable dynamics.

paragraphs: An agent trained under a limited set of conditions may encounter unfamiliar conditions at deployment. This paper argues that the sequential nature of reinforcement learning makes this generalization problem different from supervised prediction. In particular, uncertainty arising from limited knowledge can require explicit treatment because decisions unfold over time.

The authors show that generalizing to unseen conditions induces implicit partial observability, even when each underlying environment is fully observed. They formulate the resulting problem as an epistemic partially observed Markov decision process. This perspective makes uncertainty about the test conditions part of the decision problem and helps explain failure modes of algorithms that do not handle that uncertainty appropriately.

The paper then proposes a simple ensemble-based method for approximately solving the induced partially observed problem. On the Procgen benchmark suite, this approach achieves significant generalization gains over current methods. The result supports the usefulness of the epistemic POMDP formulation in the evaluated setting. More broadly, the analysis explains why uncertainty handling can be essential for reinforcement-learning generalization, even when supervised methods succeed without treating it explicitly.
neurips-2021-why-generalization-in-rl-is.tldr: Uncertainty about unseen environments induces partial observability, motivating an ensemble-based reinforcement-learning method that improves generalization on Procgen.
